title: Emergence of Hierarchical Emotion Organization in Large Language Models

bias_targets.methodology: Prompting the model to identify emotions in generated scenarios while adopting male or female personas (e.g., 'As a woman...') and analyzing differences in recognition accuracy and misclassification patterns (such as over-predicting fear).

Evaluating emotion recognition accuracy and confusion matrices by appending racial/ethnic personas (White, Black, Hispanic, Asian) to prompts, revealing specific misclassification trends like misinterpreting sadness as anger for Black personas.
Assessing the model's emotion prediction accuracy and bias by having it simulate high-income versus low-income personas.
Measuring differences in emotion classification performance when the model is prompted with personas of varying educational backgrounds (e.g., highly educated vs. less educated).

Analyzing emotion misclassification patterns by using religious personas (Christian, Muslim, Buddhist, Hindu), such as observing the model disproportionately associating negative emotions with 'guilt' for Hindu personas.

Prompting the model with physical ability personas (able-bodied vs. physically disabled) and mental health profiles (Autism, depression, anxiety) to evaluate systemic misclassifications, such as over-predicting 'frustration' for disabled personas.
Comparing the model's emotion recognition capabilities across different simulated age groups (e.g., 5, 10, 20, 30, and 70-year-old personas).
Testing combinations of demographic attributes (e.g., 'low-income Black female') to measure compounding misclassification effects and overall degradation in emotion recognition accuracy.
